summary.text: Snowball Earth is the hypothesis that during one or more icehouse climates, Earth's surface froze almost completely, with little or no liquid water exposed.
It is most often tied to the Cryogenian Period and its two major glacial episodes, the Sturtian and the Marinoan.
Supporters say it best explains glacial deposits from tropical latitudes, while opponents dispute the evidence and stress how hard it would be to escape a fully frozen state.

facts.label: Tipping point
facts.value: Glaciers within 25° to 30° of the equator

facts.label: Way out
facts.value: Volcanic CO₂ builds up into an ultra-greenhouse

items.prompt: Ice reflects sunlight. In Budyko's climate model, what happened once ice sheets pushed far enough out from the poles?

options.label: Cooling fed more ice until the whole Earth froze
The ice melted back as it reached warmer seas
The ice stopped and held a fixed line
Temperatures swung wildly with no pattern

items.explain: More ice meant more reflected sunlight, more cooling and more ice, until the planet was ice-covered and stable.

items.prompt: If the whole planet froze over, how could it ever thaw? What mechanism did Kirschvink propose?

options.label: A slow brightening of the Sun
Heat from asteroid impacts
Volcanic CO₂ piling up into a huge greenhouse effect
Ocean currents carrying warmth from the core

items.explain: Carbon dioxide from volcanic outgassing would accumulate, producing an ultra-greenhouse effect that ends the freeze.

items.prompt: Budyko's model showed a fully frozen Earth could be stable. Why did he still conclude it had never actually happened?

options.label: The Sun was too bright back then
No glacial rocks had ever been found
Oceans were too salty to freeze
His model gave no way to thaw back out

items.explain: Since his model offered no escape from the frozen state, he concluded it never happened.

items.prompt: Ancient glacial deposits turn up in lands that now sit near the tropics. Once continental drift was accepted, what simpler explanation did it offer?

options.label: The deposits were made by tropical floods
Those continents sat at higher latitudes back then
Mountain glaciers formed on very tall peaks
The deposits were carried there by sea ice

items.explain: Plate tectonics allowed the glacial sediments to have been laid down when the continents were farther from the equator.

items.prompt: Some scientists think Earth may have been a 'slushball' rather than a full snowball. What would make the difference?

options.label: Ice only at the poles, as today
A thicker ice layer at the equator
A thin band of open water near the equator
Oceans frozen, but continents bare

items.explain: A slushball would keep a thin equatorial band of open, or seasonally open, water.

items.prompt: The Snowball episodes came just before sudden bursts of new life forms. What might the most recent one have set off?

options.label: The first life on Earth
The rise of the dinosaurs
The first flowering plants
The evolution of multicellular life

items.explain: The most recent Snowball episode may have triggered the evolution of multicellularity, ahead of the Avalon and Cambrian explosions.

paragraphs.heading: A frozen planet
paragraphs.text: Snowball Earth is the idea that during one or more icehouse climates in Earth's past, almost the whole surface froze, leaving little or no open water. It is most often linked to the Cryogenian Period, which held two major glacial episodes: the Sturtian, about 717 to 660 million years ago, and the Marinoan, about 650 to 635 million years ago. One open question is whether the planet froze completely or became a 'slushball' with a thin band of open water, or seasonally open water, at the equator.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is argued over
paragraphs.text: Supporters say the idea best explains deposits thought to be glacial that formed at tropical latitudes, along with other puzzling features of the rock record. Opponents question that evidence, doubt that an ocean could really be covered in ice or slush, and stress how hard it would be to escape a fully frozen state. The episodes are placed before the Avalon and Cambrian explosions, sudden bursts of many-celled life. The latest one may have set off the evolution of multicellular life.

paragraphs.heading: The runaway ice loop
paragraphs.text: In the 1960s the Soviet climatologist Mikhail Budyko built a simple climate model based on the balance of energy. It showed that if ice spread far enough from the poles, a loop took over: ice is more reflective, a property called albedo, so the planet cooled, more ice formed, and in the end the whole Earth froze into a new stable state. Budyko concluded this had never really happened, since his model gave no way out. Modelling suggests the tipping point comes once glaciers reach within 25° to 30° of the equator, after which ice advances rapidly to the equator. So glacial deposits in the tropics hint at ice over the whole globe.

paragraphs.heading: A way out
paragraphs.text: Joseph Kirschvink coined the term 'snowball Earth' in a short paper in 1992. He noted that banded iron formations fit with such a global freeze. He also offered an escape route: volcanoes kept releasing CO₂, which built up into an ultra-greenhouse effect that let Earth break free of the ice.

paragraphs.heading: Glaciers in the tropics
paragraphs.text: Earlier, the Australian geologist Douglas Mawson found thick, widespread glacial sediments in South Australia and late in his career wondered about a global glaciation. But he wrongly assumed the continents had always stayed where they are. Continental drift and then plate tectonics offered an easier answer: the continents sat at higher latitudes when those sediments formed. Then in 1964 W. Brian Harland used palaeomagnetic data to show that glacial deposits in Svalbard and Greenland had formed at tropical latitudes, and argued for an ice age so extreme that it left marine glacial rocks in the tropics.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to prove
paragraphs.text: Testing the idea is difficult. Before the Ediacaran, the biological markers normally used to match rock layers are missing, so no one can show that rocks in different places formed at the same time. Radiometric dating, the best tool left, is seldom accurate to better than about a million years. Many features that look glacial can also form without ice, and working out where landmasses lay even 200 million years ago is hard.
